Five members of Green Environment Youth Korea (GEYK)—Kim Jin-young, Yoon Sang-ho, Lee Yu-jin, Cho Gyu-ri, and Kang Da-yeon—represented young people from South Korea at the 24th Conference of the Parties (COP24) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in Katowice, Poland.

From November 30 to December 2, we took part in the Conference of Youth (COY). We met YOUNGO for the first time, joined working groups on topics that interested us, and helped draft the position paper for the Youth Initiative.

The UN climate conference ran from December 2 to 14. Alongside our YOUNGO working groups, we attended conferences, side events, and both open and closed meetings on issues we wanted to follow.

On December 8, environmental activists and organizations from around the world joined a climate march urging negotiators to reach an agreement that would benefit the climate. People carried posters, sang, and paraded sculptures made through a civil society arts network. Their messages called for an end to coal-fired power and for action to protect people from climate change.

Reflections from the GEYK COP24 Delegation

Kang Da-yeon, university student

We have to expand what is possible for ourselves. A better world is possible.

COP exists to help address climate change by making international negotiations on climate issues succeed. If global temperatures rise by more than two degrees, the changes will threaten our ability to survive, on top of the many species we are already losing every day. We have to keep warming from exceeding 1.5 degrees. That means making enormous changes in around ten years, including changes to political, economic, and cultural problems that already exist around the world. Countries still have a long way to go to bridge their differences. The national interests politicians are unwilling to give up are tied to their citizens’ livelihoods. But what do those citizens think, and how much do we hear from them?

At COP, so many people were speaking in their own voices. Communication mattered. The climate crisis is a shared problem, so it was important to exchange ideas with people around the world and find ways to express them together. Even without extensive preparations, people can communicate effectively by wearing similar clothes, making signs, chanting, and announcing a gathering in an existing online chat. As global citizens, they found ways to put pressure on politicians. GEYK joined an action with an Asian youth environmental coalition and another with Solutions for Our Climate and people from countries where Korea had supported coal power, including the Philippines and Indonesia. Those actions and the march outside the conference were creative, sometimes joyful, and clear about who they wanted to reach. I wished it were as easy for anyone to do this in Korea.

The national pavilions sometimes felt like a display of political hypocrisy. There were few alternatives to meat, a major source of emissions. The rooms were overheated and single-use products were everywhere. Did anyone challenge those things directly? Why didn’t I? When you feel that change is needed, start with yourself. Think more deeply, pay attention to what you feel, and learn. Then work with others and speak up however you can. Those were my main lessons from COP.

We have a long way to go, but the time we have left may be shorter than we think. We have to expand what is possible for ourselves. A better world is possible.

Cho Gyu-ri, university student

Seeing climate change as a social issue through climate justice

I learned a lot at COP24. It was my first COP, and I wasn’t sure how to prepare. Just keeping track of the schedule was a challenge. I was still an undergraduate and could only attend one week of the two-week conference, which I regretted. Even so, I learned what was being discussed internationally on climate change.

My work at COP fell into three areas: attending sessions and meetings as an observer, taking part in actions, and joining a working group. I study environmental science and chemical and biomolecular engineering, so I spent more time at pavilion seminars about technologies such as renewable energy than at formal meetings. Some of the technologies still needed time to become commercially available, but I heard about approaches that hadn’t occurred to me. I joined a campaign called Human4rights. Friends from Asia and I were preparing another action, but I had to return to Korea before it took place. I also joined YOUNGO’s Renewable Energy Working Group.

What stayed with me was seeing climate change as a social issue through the idea of climate justice. Even the technology seminars and working groups I attended focused on justice and human rights. I had mainly looked at climate change from a scientific perspective before. After COP, I began to see it from social and other perspectives too.

Lee Yu-jin, university student

We have to address this human-made crisis to preserve the environment for future generations.

When we set a goal, it is just as important to work out how to achieve it. After the Paris Agreement, the parties agreed to develop its implementation guidelines by COP24 in 2018. The guidelines set out the details needed to put the agreement into practice and were as important to discuss as the agreement itself.

GEYK took part in COP24 to bring young people’s voices to the conference. During the roughly three days of the Conference of Youth before COP, we met young people and civil society representatives from other countries. We learned from each other, found motivation, and broadened our view of climate action. A youth group from the Netherlands had taken a bus from Amsterdam to Katowice instead of flying to reduce its travel emissions. Young people from Fiji, who were already seeing the effects of sea-level rise, used performances to show how serious the problem was.

Once the conference began, GEYK members worked from morning to night. We attended meetings and seminars as observers, wrote reports, and took part in working groups. At the Korea Pavilion we held a session on food security with youth organizations from Korea, China, Japan, and Taiwan. We also joined actions drawing attention to the severity of climate change and calling on parties to take stronger measures.

At the time, there were only a little over ten years until 2030 to limit the rise in global average temperatures to 1.5 degrees. We had no room to go backward. Only by making sustained progress on this human-made crisis can we preserve an environment worth leaving to future generations.

Yoon Sang-ho, working professional

I hope that energy lasts.

Three days before the 24th UN climate conference, I attended the Conference of Youth, organized by YOUNGO, the official youth constituency of the UNFCCC. COY brings young people from around the world together to prepare for COP and exchange ideas about the environment. The working groups are at its heart. Studying the issues in depth helps participants make sense of the negotiations to come. I had hoped to contribute to groups on human rights and intergenerational equity, but their meetings conflicted with seminars and I couldn’t attend as much as I wanted.

COP24 meant two weeks of packed schedules from early morning to late evening. I would arrive early, check the screen listing the day’s events, and note the meetings and seminars I wanted to attend. After two or three sessions and time to write up my notes, it would already be midnight. I was short on sleep, but it was energizing to watch experts and nonexperts find common ground and nod as they listened to one another.

If I had to describe COP24 in one word, it would be “intensity.” Government officials were caught in a sharp tug of war between protecting national interests and fulfilling their responsibilities as global citizens. Outside, people called for stronger ambition from developed and developing countries alike. Despite tangled interests, the world was slowly taking a significant step in the right direction. I sincerely hope we keep taking those steps and learn to see ourselves as part of a broader “we,” across generations and national borders.

Kim Jin-young, working professional
